query: For refractory high-entropy alloys intended for jet-turbine applications, what single intervention could improve high-temperature mechanical capability while limiting density and preserving room-temperature performance? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention, its mechanism, the expected improvement relative to a relevant baseline, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting evidence from prior studies, and a decisive experiment with a result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A slight compositional adjustment that promotes the in‐situ formation of nanoscale, ordered L21 precipitates in an otherwise single-phase BCC refractory HEA will enhance high‐temperature yield strength (via precipitation strengthening and load transfer) by roughly 15–20% over the baseline, while maintaining room‐temperature mechanical performance and keeping density low.
generation.material_initial_state: An equiatomic refractory high-entropy alloy with a single-phase BCC solid solution (e.g., a heavy-element HEA designed for high-temperature applications) without significant second-phase precipitation.
generation.intervention: Introduce a controlled, small off-stoichiometric addition of a lightweight element (e.g., aluminum) to the baseline composition to trigger the formation of fine, ordered L21 precipitates during consolidation (by adjusting processing parameters, if necessary).
generation.conditions: Tests performed under compressive loading at elevated temperatures (600–700 °C) typical of jet-turbine operating regimes, with additional confirmation via room-temperature mechanical testing.
generation.structural_mediator: Nanoscale (10–30 nm) ordered L21 precipitates homogeneously dispersed within the BCC matrix.
generation.mechanism: The nanoscale precipitates impede dislocation motion through a load transfer effect and precipitation strengthening, elevating the yield strength at high temperatures. At the same time, their controlled volume fraction and nanometric scale preserve the ductility and strength characteristics at room temperature and do not significantly increase the alloy's overall density.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline equiatomic BCC HEA, the modified alloy is expected to exhibit approximately a 15–20% improvement in yield strength at 600–700 °C while maintaining room-temperature strength and ductility; the alloy density should remain similar or slightly lower due to the addition of the lightweight element.
generation.baseline: The mechanical performance (e.g., yield strength and ductility) of the baseline equiatomic BCC refractory HEA without precipitate-forming compositional adjustments.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected only within a narrow compositional window; excessive addition of the lightweight element may lead to coarse or brittle secondary phases that could detrimentally affect room-temperature ductility or overall toughness.
generation.uncertainty: The exact volume fraction and distribution of L21 precipitates needed to optimize high-temperature performance without compromising room-temperature properties is not fully defined; the predicted improvement magnitude is estimated based on analogous precipitation-strengthened HEAs and may vary with processing conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of alloys using identical processing (e.g., mechanical alloying and spark plasma sintering): one with the baseline equiatomic BCC composition and one with a slight off-stoichiometric addition of a lightweight element (e.g., ~5 at.% Al substitution for one heavy element) intended to induce L21 precipitation. Conduct transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to verify the formation, size, and distribution of nanoscale ordered precipitates. Evaluate mechanical properties by performing compressive tests at both room temperature and at 600–700 °C.
measurements: Yield strength and ductility at room temperature and at 600–700 °C (compressive testing)
Microstructural evaluation (TEM/SEM for precipitate size, phase identification, and distribution)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if: (a) the compositional modification does not result in the formation of nanoscale, ordered L21 precipitates, or if coarse and/or brittle secondary phases form instead; or (b) the high-temperature yield strength of the modified alloy improves less than ~10% relative to the baseline or is accompanied by a significant (greater than ±5%) degradation in room-temperature performance.

cited_evidence.text: Paper card. Question: How can high-throughput computational screening be used to discover lightweight, precipitation-strengthened high-entropy alloys with high-temperature strength superior to traditional ferritic superalloys?. System: Al–Cr–Fe–Mn–Ti quinary system (specifically Al20Cr5Fe50Mn20Ti5 and Al15Cr5Fe50Mn25Ti5 as successful cases). Processing: Arc-melting of 99.9 wt% purity constituent elements, melted at least six times for homogeneity, followed by drop-casting; subsequent homogenization at 1200 °C and annealing at 700 °C for 2 hours for specific characterizations. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature and elevated temperatures (up to 700 °C) at a strain rate of 2 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹; in situ neutron scattering from room temperature to 1050 °C; synchrotron XRD and TEM characterization.
